adversarial.note: every word is a rotation of the same 10-letter multiset, so all n words share one anagram signature (one exact dict key, not merely one hash bucket) and land in a single group; empirically this does NOT degrade to O(n^2) the way distinct-but-colliding keys do, since CPython dicts resolve a repeated exact key by direct slot lookup rather than probing a chain — see README

complexity.notes: The signature is a bounded computed signature (26 counters over lowercase letters with bounded word length), so adversarial hash-collision degradation does not apply and the worst case stays linear. Inefficiency: word_tuple is computed twice per word (once building the dict, once appending); a single pass with collections.defaultdict(list) would halve the signature work. The annotation 'tuple(int)' is not valid typing syntax — 'tuple[int, ...]' was intended.
complexity.summary: Each word is mapped to a 26-element character-count tuple used as a dictionary key; words sharing a signature are appended to the same list. Word length is bounded (≤100 per constraints, 3-8 per scaling note), so each signature costs O(1) effectively and total work is O(n).

complexity.notes: Recursive implementation uses O(log n) stack space; an iterative loop would achieve O(1) space. The base cases are slightly convoluted but correct, and using the half-open [start, end) convention is clean.
complexity.summary: Classic recursive binary search over a sorted array, halving the search interval each call until the target is found or the interval is empty. No hashing involved, so average and worst case are both O(log n).

complexity.notes: The loop invariant using half-open [start, end) with early return on equality is correct; the final check handles the single-element remaining window. Slightly cleaner would be the standard left<=right formulation, but this is idiomatic and fine.
complexity.summary: Classic binary search on a sorted array, halving the search interval each iteration until the target is found or the interval is exhausted.

complexity.notes: The best_buy variable is computed but never used; it hints at the intended O(n) single-pass solution (track minimum price so far and update profit at each day). The inner loop is also redundant since the maximum sell price after i could be tracked incrementally, making this unnecessarily O(n^2).
complexity.summary: Brute force: for each buy day i, scan all later sell days j and track the maximum price difference, returning 0 if no profit exists.

complexity.notes: Initializing best_buy = 100 relies on the stated constraint prices[i] <= 100, which is a guaranteed precondition and correct; using math.inf or prices[0] would be more robust to constraint changes but is not required here.
complexity.summary: Single pass tracking the minimum price seen so far and the best profit achievable by selling at the current day. Returns the maximum of these profits, floored at 0 via the initial best_profit = 0.

complexity.notes: A debug print with math.ceil is left inside the loop and should be removed; it also wastes work since the raw float division below it is sufficient for the comparison. Popping from the end works but iterating the sorted list in reverse with an index would be more idiomatic and avoids mutating the list.
complexity.summary: Sorts cars by position, then pops from the back (closest to target first) comparing each car's arrival time to the current lead fleet's; a car with a strictly smaller arrival time starts a new fleet, otherwise it merges into the fleet ahead. Sorting dominates the running time.

complexity.notes: The 'import math' is unused. Initializing result to 1 relies on the stated constraint n >= 1, which is a guaranteed precondition, so it is safe.
complexity.summary: Sorts cars by position and scans from the car closest to the target backward, popping any car whose arrival time is no greater than the current lead fleet's (it merges into that fleet) and starting a new fleet otherwise.

complexity.notes: Per the scaling note target = 2n+1, so the O(target) allocation and filtering stay linear in n. Initializing result = 1 relies on the stated n >= 1 constraint, which is valid. Using floats for arrival-time comparison is fine here given the small integer ranges, but a cross-multiplication comparison would avoid any floating-point concern.
complexity.summary: Places cars into a counting array indexed by position (so they come out sorted), then scans from the car nearest the target, comparing arrival times to merge followers into the lead fleet and counting a new fleet whenever a car would arrive later than the lead.

complexity.notes: Starting result at 1 and unconditionally popping relies on n >= 1, which the constraints guarantee. Sorting ascending and popping from the end is a neat way to process cars nearest the target first; the float division comparison is fine within the given constraints. Under the stated scaling (target = 2n+1) the counting-array branch is essentially always taken for nontrivial n, giving linear time, and its O(target) memory stays O(n). The stray 'I asked Claude' comment should be removed.
complexity.summary: Hybrid strategy: bucket cars into a target-length counting array when target < n log n (effectively counting sort), otherwise sort by position. Then it greedily scans cars from closest-to-target outward, merging any car whose arrival time is no better than the fleet ahead of it and counting a new fleet otherwise.

complexity.notes: Storing only indices on the stack and comparing temperatures[stack[-1]] would avoid tuple allocation overhead and is slightly more idiomatic. The worst-case linear bound holds for any input, so the scaling note about bounded temperatures is not needed to justify the complexity.
complexity.summary: Monotonic decreasing stack of (temperature, index) pairs; each new temperature pops all cooler pending days and records their wait. Every index is pushed and popped at most once, so total work is linear regardless of input distribution.

adversarial.note: n distinct multiples of 2**61-1, all hashing to 0, so every dict insert/lookup collides

complexity.notes: Shadows the builtin name 'dict' with the local variable. A set with early exit on first repeated value would be simpler, use one pass, and allow early termination. Worst case degrades to O(n^2) because keys are attacker-controlled integers susceptible to adversarial hash collisions.
complexity.summary: Builds a frequency dictionary over nums in one pass, then makes a second pass to find any value with count greater than 1.

complexity.notes: Using int(a/b) routes through float division, which can lose precision for very large integers; safe here because intermediate values stay bounded (~10^6), but int(a // b * (1 if a*b >= 0 else -1)) or a trunc-toward-zero integer idiom would be more robust in general.
complexity.summary: Single pass over the tokens using a stack: push operands, and on each operator pop two operands, apply the operation, and push the result. The final stack top is the answer.

complexity.notes: The alphabet is bounded to 26 lowercase letters, so dicts hold at most 26 keys: space is O(1) and hash collisions are bounded, keeping lookups O(1) worst case. Style could be improved: a bare except is unidiomatic (KeyError should be caught explicitly, or an early length check used), the two comparison loops are redundant since equal key sets suffice, and collections.Counter(s) == collections.Counter(t) expresses the same idea more cleanly.
complexity.summary: Builds character-frequency dicts for both strings, then compares the two multisets for equality (using a bare except to catch keys missing from either side).

complexity.notes: s.lower() allocates a full copy of the string, making space O(n); using str.casefold-free in-place comparisons or lowercasing individual characters on the fly would give O(1) extra space. The inner b-loop is safe because it can never pass the already-validated alphanumeric at index a.
complexity.summary: Two-pointer scan from both ends of the lowercased string, skipping non-alphanumeric characters and comparing matching characters until the pointers meet.

complexity.notes: Clean and idiomatic; an O(1)-extra-space two-pointer variant exists, but the O(n) filtered copy is the standard readable approach.
complexity.summary: Filters the lowercased string down to alphanumeric characters, then compares the filtered string against its reverse. Each step is a single linear pass.

complexity.notes: Correctness is fine but the algorithm is impractical; the canonical monotonic-stack solution achieves the same O(n) with a small constant. Also, reusing the variable 'largest' for both the maximum bar height and the best area found is confusing — a separate variable would improve readability.
complexity.summary: Brute-force sweep: for every integer height h from 0 to max(heights), it makes one linear pass finding the widest run of bars with height >= h and tracks the best area. Since heights are bounded by 10000, this is at most 10001 linear passes, i.e. O(n) in n but with an enormous constant (~10^9 operations at n=10^5), so it will time out in practice despite being linear.

complexity.notes: Correct given the problem's length bound, but non-general and unidiomatic; Floyd's tortoise-and-hare is the standard O(n) time, O(1) space solution that works for any length.
complexity.summary: Exploits the stated constraint that the list has at most 1000 nodes: it walks at most 1005 steps, returning False if it reaches null and True (cycle must exist) otherwise. Runs in constant time and space.

complexity.notes: The set keys are ListNode objects hashed by Python's default identity hash (derived from the allocator-chosen address), so the input cannot steer collisions and lookups remain O(1) worst case. The counter variable i is unused and can be removed; Floyd's tortoise-and-hare algorithm would achieve the same result in O(1) space.
complexity.summary: Traverses the list while storing each visited ListNode in a set; if a node is seen twice a cycle exists, otherwise the walk ends at null.

adversarial.note: n distinct multiples of 2**61-1, all hashing to 0, so every set insert/lookup collides

complexity.notes: Average-case linearity depends on set hashing; adversarial integer keys can make collisions degrade lookups/removals to quadratic worst case.
complexity.summary: Build a set of the numbers, then repeatedly pop a value and expand in both directions to remove its entire consecutive run. Each distinct value is removed once, giving linear average time.

complexity.notes: Correct and O(1) extra space, but the repeated `list1.val < list2.val` checks when initializing root/next1/next2 are clunky; a dummy head node would simplify the code and avoid the duplicated comparisons. Also the final if/else both return root, so it could be collapsed to `current.next = next1 or next2; return root`.
complexity.summary: Iterative two-pointer merge: picks the smaller head as root, then walks both lists appending the smaller node each step, and finally attaches the remaining tail of whichever list is non-empty.

complexity.notes: Correctly handles duplicate minimums via the <= push condition paired with the equality-based pop. An equally idiomatic alternative stores (value, running_min) tuples on a single stack; a tuple-free variant could push 2*val - prev_min encodings, but the current approach is clearer.
complexity.summary: Two parallel stacks: the main stack holds all values, while an auxiliary min stack (seeded with +inf) pushes a value only when it is <= the current minimum and pops it when it matches the popped value, so getMin is always the top of the min stack. Every operation is O(1), and using <= with the equality check on pop correctly handles duplicate minimums.
complexity.time_average: O(1) per operation (amortized for push/pop; O(n) total for n operations)
complexity.time_worst: O(1) amortized per operation; a single push/pop can take O(n) if the underlying list reallocates, but n operations are O(n) total

complexity.notes: Uses division (prod // num), so it does not satisfy the O(n) no-division follow-up; the standard prefix/suffix product approach would. The slices nums[:zero] and nums[zero+1:] allocate O(n) extra space and could be avoided by iterating with indices. The match/case on the zero count is readable but unconventional for this problem.
complexity.summary: Counts zeros to branch into three cases: more than one zero yields all zeros; exactly one zero yields the product of non-zero elements at the zero's index; otherwise divides the total product by each element. Each case is a linear pass over the array.

complexity.notes: Clean and correct; a one-pass two-pointer (fast/slow with a gap of n) variant would avoid the length count but has the same asymptotic complexity. The `if size < 1` check is dead code given the constraint 1 <= sz.
complexity.summary: Two-pass approach: first count the list length, then use a dummy pre-head node to walk to the node just before the (size-n)th position and unlink the target node, correctly handling removal of the head.

complexity.notes: Correct but uses O(n) extra space for the node array; the classic O(1)-space approach finds the middle with slow/fast pointers, reverses the second half in place, and merges the two halves. Pointer bookkeeping in the inner loop is a bit convoluted and could be simplified.
complexity.summary: Collects all nodes into an array, then uses two pointers from both ends to rewire next pointers in the interleaved order [0, n-1, 1, n-2, ...], terminating the list at the middle.

complexity.notes: Correct but more verbose than needed; a standard `prev, curr = None, head` loop with a uniform body would handle the head and base cases without special-casing the first and last nodes.
complexity.summary: Iterative in-place reversal: walks the list once with prev/curr pointers, flipping each node's next pointer and returning the former tail as the new head.

complexity.notes: The reversal is correct (index 0 gets nodes[-1] which is None, and nodes[-2] is the old tail), but it uses O(n) extra space where the standard in-place two-pointer (prev/curr) approach achieves O(1) space. The traversal also appends a trailing None sentinel that is never really needed, and a single while-loop rewiring would be more idiomatic than the collect-then-rewire two-pass style.
complexity.summary: Collects all nodes into an auxiliary array, then rewires each node's next pointer to its predecessor and returns the former tail as the new head.

complexity.notes: Correctness relies on the delimiter never appearing inside the strings; this is guaranteed here because input strings contain only ASCII characters while the emoji is non-ASCII, but the approach fails the follow-up requirement of supporting arbitrary character sets (a length-prefix encoding would generalize). Works but is fragile and not idiomatic for a serialization problem.
complexity.summary: Encodes by joining the strings with an emoji delimiter (with a trailing delimiter to disambiguate empty strings/empty list) and decodes by splitting on that delimiter and dropping the trailing empty fragment. Both operations are linear in the total character volume, which scales linearly with the number of strings.

complexity.notes: Correctness is fragile: the constraints allow any of 256 ASCII characters, so an input string could literally contain the delimiter and corrupt the decode; a length-prefix scheme (e.g. 'len#string') is the robust standard approach. Works only because real inputs are unlikely to contain the magic string. Also, decode relies on the trailing delimiter to make pop(-1) valid, which is a bit subtle.
complexity.summary: Encodes by joining all strings with a long fixed literal delimiter (plus a trailing delimiter) and decodes by splitting on that delimiter and dropping the final empty piece. Both join and split are linear in the total character volume, which scales linearly with n.

complexity.notes: The repeated slicing in decode causes the O(n^2) behavior; using an index pointer into the original string (and only materializing each extracted word) would restore O(n) total time. Also, int(s[0:a]) is computed twice per iteration — parse it once into a variable for readability.
complexity.summary: Encodes each string as '<len>|<string>' concatenated together; decode repeatedly finds the '|' delimiter, parses the length, and extracts the payload. Encode is linear in total characters, but decode re-slices the remaining string each iteration (s = s[...:]), copying the suffix each time, which makes the whole decode quadratic in the total character volume.

adversarial.note: n distinct multiples of 2**61-1, all hashing to 0, so every dict insert/lookup collides

complexity.notes: The input range -1000..1000 bounds the distinct keys to a constant 2001, so the sort, the per-count dict scans, and any hash collisions are all constant-bounded; space is likewise O(1). Style-wise the reverse lookup (scanning items for each top count and deduping with set()) is fragile and unidiomatic; heapq.nlargest or Counter.most_common on (key, count) pairs would be clearer and avoid the repeated scans.
complexity.summary: Counts frequencies in a dict, sorts the distinct frequency values, takes the top k counts, then finds the keys matching those counts by scanning the dict for each of the k counts, deduplicating via a set.

adversarial.note: n distinct multiples of 2**61-1, all hashing to 0, so every dict insert/lookup collides

complexity.notes: No hashing is used, so worst case is genuinely O(n log n) from the sort; the index() calls are O(n) each but only a constant number of them. The index-recovery logic is convoluted and fragile — storing (value, index) pairs before sorting or using a hash map would be both simpler and O(n) average time. Also note nums.index may misidentify which of two equal-valued elements was picked, though the single-solution guarantee prevents wrong output.
complexity.summary: Copies and sorts the array, then uses a two-pointer scan from both ends to find the pair summing to target, and finally recovers the original indices via linear index() lookups (with a pop workaround for duplicate values).

adversarial.note: n distinct multiples of 2**61-1 (already ascending), all hashing to 0, so every dict insert/lookup collides

complexity.notes: The input is guaranteed sorted, so sorting is wasted work and forces an awkward value-to-index remapping; a direct two-pointer scan on nums would be O(n) time and O(1) space. As written, nums2 is an O(n) copy, violating the problem's O(1) extra-space requirement, and mutating nums with pop is poor style. The O(n) index/pop calls are dominated by the sort, so the bound stands.
complexity.summary: Needlessly copies and sorts the already-sorted array (Timsort O(n log n)), then runs an O(n) two-pointer scan on the copy, and finally maps values back to original indices with O(n) list.index calls (plus an O(n) pop to disambiguate duplicates).

complexity.notes: Using list.count inside the loop gives O(k^2) per line (fine at k=9, but a set-based single pass would be cleaner and scalable). The `valid *= isValidLine(...)` trick works but is unidiomatic — prefer `valid = valid and ...` or `all()` with a generator. Also, the board could be validated in one pass over all 81 cells rather than three separate loops.
complexity.summary: Validates each row, column, and 3x3 box by checking for duplicate non-empty cells using list.count. Since the board is always 9x9, all work is bounded by constants (81 cells, each line scan doing up to 9 count operations of length 9).

complexity.notes: No hashing is used (membership test is on a 3-element list), so the O(n) bound holds in the worst case. Correct but slightly clunky: a dict mapping closers to openers would avoid the repetitive elif chain; also note each elif pops exactly once, so there is no double-pop bug, but the style invites one.
complexity.summary: Classic stack-based validation: push opening brackets, and on each closing bracket check that the popped top matches the corresponding opening type; the string is valid iff the stack is empty at the end.

complexity.notes: The dict keys are a fixed three-character literal, so lookups are O(1) worst case with no adversarial hash risk. Idiomatic and clean; iterating while indexing the map directly is fine since the input is guaranteed to contain only bracket characters.
complexity.summary: Classic stack-based validation: push each opening bracket, and for each closing bracket pop and check it matches via a fixed closing-to-opening map. Returns true only if every close matches and the stack empties.
